name: Non-Linear Factor Models
title: Non-Linear Factor Models
answer: Non-linear factor models describe asset returns as a function of predictors where the relationship can include interactions, thresholds, and regime-dependent effects that linear factor models miss. In quantitative trading they are used to build return forecasts, decompose risk, and construct portfolios across equities, futures, and currencies. The scope covers both cross-sectional models that rank assets at a point in time and time-series models that capture changing exposures. These models sit between traditional linear factor work and fully unstructured deep learning, and they are evaluated against linear benchmarks for marginal predictive value.

sections.body: Non-linear factor models describe asset returns as a function of predictors where the relationship can include interactions, thresholds, and regime-dependent effects that linear factor models miss. In quantitative trading they are used to build return forecasts, decompose risk, and construct portfolios across equities, futures, and currencies. The scope covers both cross-sectional models that rank assets at a point in time and time-series models that capture changing exposures. These models sit between traditional linear factor work and fully unstructured deep learning, and they are evaluated against linear benchmarks for marginal predictive value.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on historical market data, point-in-time fundamentals, and often alternative data such as news sentiment or order flow, all stored in time-aligned databases. Model training typically uses distributed compute with GPU or CPU clusters, while live signal generation may require low-latency inference close to execution. Backtesting engines replay data with realistic transaction costs, corporate actions, and survivorship bias controls. Feature stores and experiment tracking systems keep inputs and model versions reproducible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners estimate non-linear factor models with methods such as gradient boosted trees, random forests, kernel ridge regression, splines, or shallow neural networks. Features are built from lagged returns, valuation ratios, momentum, volatility, and macro variables, often with interaction terms or embeddings for categorical data. Training uses walk-forward validation, regularization, and ensemble averaging to reduce overfitting. Model outputs are typically converted to scores or expected returns and then passed to a portfolio optimizer with constraints.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Model risk management requires independent validation, documentation of data provenance, and monitoring for performance decay or regime shifts. Overfitting is a central concern, so backtests are stress-tested with multiple scenarios and out-of-sample periods. Interpretability tools such as Shapley values or partial dependence plots are used to explain factor contributions to risk committees. Data licensing, code versioning, and audit trails support reproducibility and compliance with market conduct rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward hybrid models that combine linear factor structure with non-linear residuals, preserving interpretability while capturing complex effects. Time-series transformers and graph neural networks are being explored for cross-asset and lead-lag relationships. Causal inference methods are gaining attention to separate predictive signals from spurious correlations. Regulatory and internal governance pressure is pushing for more explainable and continuously monitored non-linear models.
